articles.title: Young people: are you doom-saving or doom-spending? How are you approaching the future?
articles.summary: We want to hear from people under 30 about how you feel about the future and whether it’s changed the way you live your life, for better or worse. The future feels a little hard to plan for right now.
body: We’ve just lived through the hottest summer on record, global conflict looms large and AI has people wondering whether their job will still exist in five years – assuming they’ve got one in the first place.
So, with all that hanging over us, are young people simply thinking: we might as well enjoy ourselves while we can?
Or perhaps all this uncertainty has made you more cautious, more focused on getting your finances in order and determined to build a future you can rely on.
Whatever your approach, we want to hear from you. How has the state of the world changed the way you live your life?

articles.title: Your dog is bored. Here are the best tools, toys, and tips in the US to keep them enriched
articles.summary: From indoor scent training to the longest-lasting slow feeders, these are experts’ top recommendations for keeping dogs fulfilled. The best toys and tools in the US for bored indoor cats. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: A dog is much more than just a pet. They’re like family, the most eager companions for your big adventures and then the best accompaniment for an evening of snuggling up on the couch and whittling away at your Netflix queue.

At least, that’s the ideal situation. In the real world, a dog who gets too little attention and exercise or, on the flip side, is over-stimulated or over-tired, can be a real problem. There are lots of warning signs, such as a dog that is overly antsy or destructive, but Suzanne Clothier, an expert dog trainer and author of numerous books on dog enrichment, sums it up in a very simple way: “Can you watch TV or read a book in peace? If not, the dog’s telling you something.”

While there’s no one-button fix for a bored dog, advancements in enrichment toys and training are making it easier to give your little pal a fulfilled life. We spoke with five certified dog experts to get their favorite tips, tricks, toys and techniques to bolster your best buddy’s confidence and attitude.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this sweltering summer, I finally stopped giving a tuck
articles.summary: I’ve always cinched my outfits at the waist, but shifting to a looser silhouette has helped me keep my cool in more ways than one. This was the summer of the Great Untuck.
body: This was the summer of the Great Untuck. The long hot summer of 2026 finally taught me to do what fashion has been nagging me about for years, which is to quit tucking in my shirts and T-shirts. To stop assuming that the top half of an outfit must be neatly cinched by the waistband of the skirt or trousers.

It wasn’t a style epiphany, to be fair. It was just too hot to do anything else. An extended run of hot weather at home changes how you dress. In the old-school type of British heatwave, which lasted about half a week, I was too giddy with excitement at not having to wear a cardigan to think more strategically. But this summer was different. And eventually I discovered what hot-climate cultures have always known, which is that loose, generously sized clothing that maximises sun protection while minimising skin contact is way more pleasant to wear in the heat than anything short and tight.

articles.title: ‘Dress good to run fast’: How Black athletes became style icons
articles.summary: From Naomi Osaka’s NBA-inspired entrance to Dennis Rodman’s punk aesthetic, Black sportspeople have long used fashion to express identity, defiance and joy. When Long Wave lead writer Nesrine Malik asked me if I’d seen Japanese-Haitian tennis star Naomi Osaka’s incredible pre-match look, I began to…
body: The star isn’t the first to acquire as many headlines for her clothes as for her performance. Osaka draws on a long tradition of Black athletes giving crowds their money’s worth through playful and provocative fashion statements. I delved into the history of why so many Black communities have a culture of “presenting”, and how defiance through fashion has found a natural home in sport.

Growing up, were you told you had to “present”? I’m talking about having elbows and knees moisturised, neat hair, a colour-coordinated outfit and matching underwear, just in case you had to go into hospital unexpectedly. In many Black cultures across the diaspora, it is far better to be overdressed than underdressed, and “extra” is more a term of endearment than an accusation. A considered, extravagant or playful outfit enters into a kind of shared visual language, and there is a culture of “turning out”, of giving the people a bit of a spectacle.

Better year, however, is what all of these A-listers will be wearing on the step and repeat for the splashy premieres. articles.title: How Fashion Week Forgot Its Black Inspiration
articles.summary: As early as 1969, Ophelia DeVore was putting on runway shows in Bryant Park hailed as “fashion extravaganzas” by The Amsterdam News, New York’s Black newspaper of record.
body: But that’s not what makes the dress interesting. After all, it’s just one of five frocks the Smithsonian retains from DeVore’s closet—31 pieces in all, mostly accessories.

Tucked at the bottom of this particular dress’s display placard is a curious subheading: The Roots of New York Fashion Week. “With her Grace Del Marco models, DeVore created innovative fashion shows in Bryant Park in New York City,” the placard reads. “Each summer during lunchtime, her multicultural models walked the runway in Bryant Park. The shows were so impressive that white marketers decided to appropriate the shows, adding tents and inviting top designers worldwide to show their fashions.”

What makes the text provocative—not least of all because of the Smithsonian’s touchstone status in President Donald Trump’s war on DEI —is that its claim is uncharacteristically vague. What years? What models? What designers? What marketers? The museum’s media specialist in its public affairs office could not answer. She declined phone interview requests.

The Quest Pro uses a balanced halo-style strap with the battery placed at the back, which spreads the weight more evenly than front-heavy headsets. The displays push 1,920 by 1,800 pixels per eye, with better contrast and richer colors thanks to local dimming. articles.title: Who Shows Up—and Who Vanishes—When Your Kid Is in Trouble?
articles.summary: Does bad luck feel contagious, as though it might somehow infect the people who used to recognize their own family lives and routines in mine?
body: The first time my friend Leucas visited us, it was a cold and dark January in Canada, but we made the most of it. Leucas learned the art of layering pants to defeat the chill; they taught my eight-year-old daughter, Rose, to ice skate; and we ate butter tarts near the water.

Nine months later, Leucas came back—but this visit was different. They flew from L.A. to Toronto with only a few hours’ notice, and during our long days together, we hardly spoke. Instead, Leucas spent the duration taking care of my one-year-old, Calvin, while I coordinated Rose’s medical care.

It had started a few days earlier, with seizure-like movements—then, everything else changed. Rose’s eyes, usually bright, couldn’t focus on us. They were dilated and wild. Over the next few hours, she lost the ability to use the toilet, speak, walk, sleep, or eat. My husband David eventually moved with her into the basement, where she wailed for hours on end as she experienced new and agonizing neurological symptoms.
points: Does bad luck feel contagious, as though it might somehow infect the people who used to recognize their own family lives and routines in mine?
